title: Janmashtami (midnight; Krishna's birth)
hook: a whole house awake at a quarter to twelve, a tiny cradle, and a fast that breaks at midnight
tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri as it's kept: a pot, sprouting barley, circles of dancers, dolls on steps. Your line was name the seed you planted.

It's eleven forty-five at night, and nobody in the house is asleep. The kids were supposed to be in bed hours ago; they're wide awake. Grandma hasn't eaten since morning. In the corner is a tiny wooden cradle hung with flowers, and in it a little image of a baby. The temple down the road is packed, and people are singing the same few lines over and over, louder as the minutes pass. Someone is watching the clock. At midnight, the conch shells blow, the bells go wild, and everyone shouts. Nothing happened, and everything did. This is Janmashtami. You heard the night itself on day ninety-two; today, how it's kept.
screen: `ELEVEN FORTY-FIVE. NOBODY'S ASLEEP.` → `A CRADLE WITH FLOWERS.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THE CONCH.`

segments.voice: The story, from the Bhagavata Purana: Krishna born at midnight in Kamsa's prison, carried across the flooded Yamuna, hidden among cowherds. Janma, birth. Ashtami, the eighth day of the dark half of the month, usually in August or September. The festival turns that story into a night you live through. First, the fast. Many people eat nothing, or only fruit and milk, from morning until midnight. It isn't a punishment. It's waiting, with your body. Second, the night. Temples and homes stay awake, singing bhajans and retelling the story, sometimes acting it out, so by midnight you've walked the whole road from the prison to the river. Third, the moment. At midnight the image of baby Krishna is bathed like a newborn, in milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar mixed together: panchamrita, the five nectars. He's dressed in new clothes and laid in the cradle, and people take turns giving it a push. Then the food, often sweets made with butter, because the baby Krishna of the stories is a famous butter thief. And the fast breaks. All evening, the children have their own part. In many homes and schools, small boys and girls are dressed as Krishna, with a peacock feather in the hair and a little flute, and temples set up jhankis, small scenes of the story, the prison, the river, the cradle, for people to walk past and look at. You can't make midnight come faster. You can only stay awake, and be ready when it does.
screen: `JANMA, BIRTH. ASHTAMI, THE EIGHTH.` · `A FAST: WAITING WITH YOUR BODY.` · `THE BATH, THE CRADLE, THE PUSH.` · `A PEACOCK FEATHER, A LITTLE SCENE.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE, AND BE READY.`

segments.voice: Picture that tiny cradle hung with flowers, in a room full of people who've waited all day, and give it one small push: breathe out as it swings away, breathe in as it comes back, gently, because there's a newborn in there. If you pray, say Krishna's name once with each swing. If not, just keep the rhythm, and wait with everyone else.
Janmashtami. Krishna's birth, on the eighth day of the dark half of the month, kept with a fast, a vigil, and a cradle rocked at midnight.
Your line: stay awake, and be ready. Midnight comes when it comes. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing and retell Krishna's birth in homes and temples, and at midnight bathe an image of baby Krishna in panchamrita, dress him, and rock him in a cradle before breaking the fast; children are often dressed as Krishna, and temples set up jhankis, small scenes of the story.

chat.says: Why does everyone stay up until midnight on Janmashtami?
options: Krishna was born at midnight, so people fast, sing and wait, then rock his cradle.
That's when Krishna lifted the hill, so people stay up to remember it.
Midnight is when Krishna left the cowherds, so people stay up to see him off.
chat.meaning: Janmashtami keeps Krishna's midnight birth: a fast, a vigil of songs and story, then the baby bathed and laid in the cradle at midnight.

notes: Date: Krishna Paksha Ashtami of Bhadrapada (purnimanta) / Shravana (amanta), usually August–September. Confirm.
Panchamrita composition (milk, curd, honey, ghee, sugar) varies slightly by family. Confirm.
Fasting until midnight: many fast fully (nirjala) or with fruit and milk (phalahar). Confirm.
Dahi handi (Gopalkala) in Maharashtra on the day after. Confirm.
